text: A counts dictionary like 00: 503, 11: 521 is correct but hard to read at a glance. plot_histogram turns it into the bar chart you'd actually put in a report or a slide.

Once you have a counts dictionary from a run, visualizing it is one import and one function call. plot_histogram takes the dictionary you already know how to read and draws one vertical bar per bitstring that appears in it. The x-axis lists the measured outcomes, the y-axis is the raw count or the normalized probability. There's no new data here, just a layout a human can scan by bar height instead of dictionary values.
Here's real output from Qiskit's own documentation: one bar per present bitstring, sized by count or probability, with nothing drawn for an outcome that never occurred.

Take the Bell-state circuit's real seeded run: 00 at 503, 11 at 521, with 01 and 10 at zero. Both bars reach roughly the middle of the chart, close to the 50% line, close to each other but not pixel-identical — the normal shot-noise wobble around a true 50/50 split. Critically, there's no bar at all for 01 or 10 — not a bar at zero height, but a complete absence, because plot_histogram only draws bars for keys present in the dictionary with a nonzero count.

The more common real question isn't just what one run produced, it's whether run B looked different from run A. plot_histogram supports this directly by accepting a list of counts dictionaries with a legend, drawing paired bars at each bitstring position — the practical day-to-day way to make noise, calibration drift, or parameter changes visible in one glance.
Next lesson maps a single qubit's state to something even more direct than a bar chart: a single 3D arrow on the Bloch sphere, where every gate you've learned becomes a visible rotation.
